title: Dario Amodei was OpenAI’s research director in 2019 when the team (with his involvement) initially withheld the full GPT-2 model, calling it too dangerous to release due to risks like misinformation a
content:
Dario Amodei was OpenAI’s research director in 2019 when the team (with his involvement) initially withheld the full GPT-2 model, calling it too dangerous to release due to risks like misinformation and misuse. 

He specifically pushed the view that the world needed time to prepare. It was a staged, cautious rollout.

Yet Anthropic (and Dario) have aggressively developed and released increasingly powerful models like Claude, while simultaneously lobbying hard for regulations, transparency mandates, and export controls that disproportionately burden competitors or smaller players. 

This is classic regulatory capture: using government levers to create a moat, positioning themselves as the safe frontrunner who gets to help write the rules, while racing ahead.

Recent events show the backfire

•Anthropic pushed for stronger government powers to audit, test, and even block unsafe frontier models (e.g., Dario’s recent calls for an FAA for AI with authority to halt releases).

•They highlighted risks in their own Mythos/Fable-class models.

•The US government then used export controls to force Anthropic to disable access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 worldwide over jailbreak/cyber concerns, exactly the kind of intervention they invited.

This looks less like principled safety advocacy and more like a strategy to lock in advantages (e.g., via export controls favoring incumbents, state-level rules, or compliance burdens) that ultimately turned around and bit them.

OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 apparently dodged similar treatment, highlighting the selective and inconsistent application the original post complained about.
It’s a textbook case of inviting the regulatory state in as a partner, only for it to act like a regulator when it suits broader (or political) priorities.

Dario’s early caution on GPT-2 was consistent with safety concerns, and the boy who cried wolf marketing, Anthropic playbook, safety rhetoric plus heavy policy engagement, has invited exactly this kind of blowback. 

The good faith engagement narrative ignores how self-serving the lobbying often appears.

content:
258個の AI が同時にコードを審査して、かかったコストはコーヒー数杯分だった。

Claude Code を、DeepSeek など 337 以上のモデルに向け直せるツールが公開された。名前は Deep-Claude。

Claude Code のリクエストを横取りして、安いモデルに転送するだけ。本物の Claude Code の設定ファイルは一切触らない。

ただの「別 AI への切り替えアプリ」ではない。
それっぽい「API 呼び出しのラッパー」でもない。

Deep-Claude は、258 エージェントを並列で動かすような大規模なワークフローでも使えるほど安定している。

実測値がこれ。

→ 1000 万トークン以上を処理
→ Claude の高性能モデルなら同じ処理で約 7.5 万円（$500 相当）
→ DeepSeek を使えばそれをはるかに下回るコストで完了
→ 34 分 33 秒で 258 エージェントが並列処理

これまで「Claude Code を動かすとすぐ課金が積み上がる」という感覚があった場面を、「安いモデルをその場で使い分ける」に変える。

複数のエージェントが同時に違うモデルを使う混在構成も動く。

導入もシンプル。

git clone してインストールスクリプトを実行、OpenRouter（モデルの中継サービス）の API キーを入力するだけ。

・MIT ライセンス（無料・商用利用可）
・本物の Claude Code 設定を上書きしない
・337 以上のモデルから選択可能（DeepSeek / Gemini / GPT / Grok / Qwen など）

詳しくは下に置きます。

content:
This is going to be revolutionary😳

In 12 months, manually managing your inbox will look as outdated as manually sorting files on your desktop.

Most people haven't realized it yet.

They're still:

• writing the same replies
• forgetting follow-ups
• searching for old threads
• checking calendars before every response

AI shouldn't just write emails.

It should run email.

That's what caught my attention about @slashyemail 

It learns your communication style, drafts replies, tracks follow-ups, understands context, and handles the repetitive inbox work that quietly steals hours every week.

One of those products that feels obvious the moment you see it.

Bookmark this tweet and come back in 6 months.

Link in comments 👇

content:
Google DeepMind quietly published a paper 4 days ago asking the question everyone skipped past:

What happens *after* AGI?

Not "when does AGI arrive." What does AGI build next.

It's called "From AGI to ASI." 14 senior DeepMind researchers, including co-founder Shane Legg and Marcus Hutter, who built the foundational theory it leans on.

Their definition of superintelligence is the part that reframes everything. ASI isn't "smarter than a smart human." They define it as a machine that outperforms not just individual experts but large, well-coordinated groups of them across nearly every field.

Not a genius. An entire institution's worth of cognition, in one system.

They lay out four pathways to get there:

→ **Scaling** — keep pumping compute and data into current models
→ **Paradigm shifts** — new architectures that replace what we use today
→ **Recursive improvement** — AI that improves its own intelligence
→ **Multi-agent collectives** — many AIs coordinating into something greater than any one of them

But here's what the hype threads are leaving out, and what makes this paper actually worth reading:

It spends just as much time on the limits. The report includes a sober list of what superintelligence cannot do, no matter how smart it gets. Even ASI stays bound by physics — the speed of light still caps how fast information travels. It's as much about friction and bottlenecks as it is about acceleration.

The central claim is the unsettling one: AI progress is unlikely to stall at human level.

And the popular image of one dramatic "step change" the day AGI arrives? Probably wrong. Superintelligence is more likely to come as a series of transformative advances rolling across science and technology.

A frontier lab is no longer treating the world beyond human-level AI as science fiction.

They're treating it as a research problem to map now.
